evidence.cite: McKeefry DJ, Zeki S. The position and topography of the human colour centre as revealed by functional magnetic resonance imaging. Brain. 1997;120(Pt 12):2229-42.

evidence.claim: Ventral occipital lesions cause cerebral achromatopsia, with other visual loss
evidence.finding: A meta-analysis of 92 case reports found that nearly all cases showed some deficit in colour discrimination and almost all showed some loss of spatial vision. Lesion overlap was highest in a small region of ventral occipital cortex, near sites that imaging links to colour.
evidence.quote: To address these issues, we performed a meta-analysis of 92 case reports from the literature. The severity of color vision deficits of the cases varied greatly, although nearly all showed some deficit in color discrimination.
evidence.cite: Bouvier SE, Engel SA. Behavioral deficits and cortical damage loci in cerebral achromatopsia. Cereb Cortex. 2006;16(2):183-91.

hint: motion area near where the temporal, parietal and occipital lobes meet
summary: Area MT, also called V5, is a small visual area at the border of the occipital and temporal lobes, near the temporo-parieto-occipital junction, that is specialized for visual motion. It is drawn here from HCP area MT. Most of its neurons are direction-selective, and they are organized in columns for direction of motion. It receives from V1, V2 and V3 and sends to the parietal cortex and the frontal eye field. Damage causes akinetopsia, the loss of motion perception.
where: It lies on the lateral occipitotemporal surface, near the junction of the inferior temporal sulcus and the lateral occipital sulcus, in the region of the temporo-parieto-occipital junction. It sits just in front of the lateral occipital complex, which abuts it behind. On the model it lies on the lateral surface at the back, and is found best in a lateral view.
does: MT is the motion area of the dorsal stream. Its neurons respond to the direction and speed of moving stimuli, and activity in MT matches perceived motion, even when motion is illusory, as in the waterfall illusion. Stimulating directionally tuned clusters in monkey MT biases the animal's judgement of motion direction, which shows that MT activity helps cause motion perception. In humans, TMS over V5 abolishes motion perception at a short, precise delay.
connects: It receives input from V1 (layer 4B), V2 and V3, as well as a direct route from the pulvinar and the lateral geniculate nucleus. It projects to the neighbouring medial superior temporal area, the lateral intraparietal area and the frontal eye field, which use motion for eye movements.
clinical: Bilateral lesions that include the lateral temporo-occipital cortex cause akinetopsia, as in the patient who could not see movement in depth, and saw moving things as a series of still frames. She also had trouble pouring a cup of tea, because she could not track the rising level. Movement perception by sound and touch was unaffected.
remember: V5 and MT are one: the motion spot, whose loss makes the world a stack of snapshots.
facts: MT is also called V5, and its neurons are strongly direction-selective.
TMS to V5 abolishes motion perception at a delay near the onset of the stimulus.
Akinetopsia was described in a patient with bilateral lateral temporo-occipital lesions.

quiz.q: Which small occipitotemporal area, called V5, holds neurons tuned to the direction of visual motion?
A patient with bilateral lateral temporo-occipital damage sees moving objects as still frames. Which area is lost?
Which area near the temporo-parieto-occipital junction lies just in front of the lateral occipital complex?

how_we_know: MT is among the best-supported areas because lesion, imaging, TMS and monkey stimulation all agree. The human lesions are large and bilateral and rarely limited to MT, but TMS offers a reversible causal test in healthy people.

evidence.claim: Bilateral lateral temporo-occipital damage selectively disturbs the perception of movement
evidence.finding: A patient with bilateral posterior brain damage had a nearly pure loss of movement vision. She had no impression of movement in depth, and could only tell stationary from moving targets in the periphery. Movement perceived through sound and touch was normal, and the damage affected the lateral temporo-occipital cortex.
evidence.quote: A patient who suffered bilateral posterior brain damage exhibited disturbance of movement vision in a rather pure form.
evidence.cite: Zihl J, von Cramon D, Mai N. Selective disturbance of movement vision after bilateral brain damage. Brain. 1983;106(Pt 2):313-40.

evidence.claim: PET picks out V5 near the temporo-parieto-occipital junction for visual motion
evidence.finding: PET compared moving with stationary black and white patterns. A unique area was identified in the region of the temporo-parieto-occipital junction, area V5, while a colour contrast found V4 elsewhere. This is correlational.
evidence.quote: The comparison identified a unique area located in the region of the temporo-parieto-occipital junction (area V5).
evidence.cite: Zeki S, Watson JD, Lueck CJ, Friston KJ, et al. A direct demonstration of functional specialization in human visual cortex. J Neurosci. 1991;11(3):641-9.

evidence.claim: MT activity tracks the illusory motion of the waterfall illusion
evidence.finding: In fMRI, human MT responded better to moving than to stationary stimuli, and activity rose when subjects viewed a stationary stimulus that appeared to move after adaptation. The fMRI time course matched the time course of the aftereffect measured in parallel, and the effect was smaller or absent in five other retinotopic areas.
evidence.quote: Here we demonstrate a clear increase in activity in MT when subjects viewed a stationary stimulus undergoing illusory motion, following adaptation to stimuli moving in a single local direction.
evidence.cite: Tootell RB, Reppas JB, Dale AM, Look RB, et al. Visual motion aftereffect in human cortical area MT revealed by functional magnetic resonance imaging. Nature. 1995;375(6527):139-41.

evidence.claim: TMS over V5 abolishes motion perception much more than TMS over V1 does
evidence.finding: In healthy people, TMS over V5 at a delay near the visual stimulus onset abolished the ability to discriminate motion direction, while TMS over V1 abolished it only marginally and at later delays. The timing suggests signals reach V5 before V1 through a fast route that bypasses V1.
evidence.quote: We conclude (i) that stimulation of V5 is a much more potent way of inducing akinetopsia (motion imperception) than stimulation of V1;
evidence.cite: Beckers G, Zeki S. The consequences of inactivating areas V1 and V5 on visual motion perception. Brain. 1995;118(Pt 1):49-60.

stimulation.method: transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over V5 in healthy volunteers
stimulation.effect: A pulse over V5 at the right moment abolished the perception of motion direction, a temporary akinetopsia. A pulse over V1 had only a marginal effect at later delays.
stimulation.quote: We conclude (i) that stimulation of V5 is a much more potent way of inducing akinetopsia (motion imperception) than stimulation of V1;
stimulation.cite: Beckers G, Zeki S. The consequences of inactivating areas V1 and V5 on visual motion perception. Brain. 1995;118(Pt 1):49-60.

hint: side of the occipital lobe, behind MT, responds to objects
summary: The lateral occipital complex is a region of lateral occipital and posterior ventral temporal cortex that responds more to objects than to textures or scrambled images. It lies just behind area MT and is drawn here from HCP areas LO1, LO2 and LO3, which are retinotopic visual field maps, so the outline approximates the functionally defined LOC. It sits in the ventral stream between early visual areas and the temporal cortex. It carries information about object shape that does not depend on the exact contours. TMS to this region impairs object recognition but not recognition of faces or bodies.
where: It lies on the lateral surface of the occipital lobe, extending into the posterior parts of the inferior temporal and fusiform gyri, just behind and below area MT. The model uses HCP areas LO1, LO2 and LO3, which are visual field maps on the lateral occipital cortex, so the outline approximates the functional LOC, which also reaches the ventral surface. A lateral view shows it best.
does: The LOC responds more to images of objects than to textures, even when power spectra match, and its response does not change with size or with whether the eyes scan the object. Its adaptation tracks perceived shape, not the contours drawn, and its activity follows how recognizable an object is. It is not tied to the semantic stage of recognition, because famous faces, common objects and unfamiliar sculptures activate it about equally. It is an intermediate step between feature analysis and recognition.
connects: It receives input from V1 to V4 and the retinotopic lateral occipital maps, and projects to the fusiform gyrus, the inferior temporal cortex and the parietal cortex. It lies in the ventral stream, and parts of it also communicate with dorsal stream regions.
clinical: Bilateral lesions of lateral occipital cortex cause visual form agnosia: in patient D.F., fMRI showed no object-selective response in the LO, and her lesion matched the LO location, yet the grasp network in the dorsal stream still worked. Damage here leaves colour and motion perception better preserved. TMS over right LO impairs object discrimination.
remember: LOC is the object spot behind MT: shapes light it up, textures do not.
facts: The LOC responds more to objects than to textures matched in power spectra.
TMS over right LO impaired object discrimination but not discrimination of faces or bodies.
Patient D.F. had bilateral lesions where LO lies, and form agnosia with preserved visually guided grasping.

quiz.q: Which lateral occipital region responds more to objects than to textures and represents perceived shape?
Patient D.F. could not recognize drawings but grasped objects well. Which region, lesioned bilaterally, lacked object-selective activation?
Which object-selective cortex abuts the back of area MT on the lateral occipital surface?

how_we_know: The LOC was found with fMRI, and then tested with TMS and with the lesion in patient D.F. The three methods agree that it supports object shape, but the HCP outline is a retinotopic approximation of a region defined by function.

evidence.claim: A lateral occipital region responds more to objects than to textures
evidence.finding: In the fMRI study that named the lateral occipital complex, activation was at the lateral-posterior occipital lobe just behind MT/V5. It was stronger for objects than for textures, including textures matched in power spectra but randomized in phase, and it was not changed by size or eye movements.
evidence.quote: LO showed preferential activation to images of objects, compared to a wide range of texture patterns.
evidence.cite: Malach R, Reppas JB, Benson RR, Kwong KK, et al. Object-related activity revealed by functional magnetic resonance imaging in human occipital cortex. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 1995;92(18):8135-9.

evidence.claim: The LOC represents perceived object shape, not simple image contours
evidence.finding: An event-related fMRI adaptation experiment showed adaptation in the LOC when perceived shape was the same but the contours differed. There was no adaptation when contours were the same but the perceived shape differed. This means the LOC represents higher level shape information.
evidence.quote: We found adaptation in the LOC when perceived shape was identical but contours differed, but not when contours were identical but perceived shape differed.
evidence.cite: Kourtzi Z, Kanwisher N. Representation of perceived object shape by the human lateral occipital complex. Science. 2001;293(5534):1506-9.

evidence.claim: A bilateral lesion at LO leaves object recognition impaired and grasping spared
evidence.finding: Patient D.F. has severe visual form agnosia. In fMRI she showed no difference between line drawings of objects and scrambled drawings in the lateral occipital cortex, which responded in healthy people, and high-resolution MRI showed her lesion matched the LO location on both sides. Her dorsal stream activated normally for grasping.
evidence.quote: Moreover, high-resolution anatomical MRI showed that her lesion corresponded bilaterally with the location of LO in healthy participants.
evidence.cite: James TW, Culham J, Humphrey GK, Milner AD, et al. Ventral occipital lesions impair object recognition but not object-directed grasping: an fMRI study. Brain. 2003;126(Pt 11):2463-75.

evidence.claim: TMS over right LO impairs object discrimination but not faces or bodies
evidence.finding: TMS was delivered over three adjacent functionally localized areas while participants discriminated faces, bodies and objects. Stimulation of right LO impaired objects but not faces or bodies, over the occipital face area impaired faces only, and over the extrastriate body area impaired bodies only.
evidence.quote: TMS over rLO impaired discrimination of objects but not faces or bodies.
evidence.cite: Pitcher D, Charles L, Devlin JT, Walsh V, et al. Triple dissociation of faces, bodies, and objects in extrastriate cortex. Curr Biol. 2009;19(4):319-24.

stimulation.method: transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over right lateral occipital area (rLO)
stimulation.effect: TMS over right LO impaired discrimination of objects, but not of faces or bodies.
stimulation.quote: TMS over rLO impaired discrimination of objects but not faces or bodies.
stimulation.cite: Pitcher D, Charles L, Devlin JT, Walsh V, et al. Triple dissociation of faces, bodies, and objects in extrastriate cortex. Curr Biol. 2009;19(4):319-24.
